paragraphs.text: The Thanksgiving table can feel like the dance floor of a throbbing nightclub. “Play the hits!” the crowd roars. This is not the time for experimental synths or clunky transitions. “Tradition” — that fraught and flimsy word — sets the tempo. But who gets to control the D.J. booth?

Often, it’s the host, determined by age or authority — and bedroom-to-bathroom ratio. Certainly my cozy apartment looks cramped in the shadow of Thanksgiving, its quaint four-seat dining table shy about half a dozen place settings.

So my fellow single 30-somethings — members of a generation struggling to afford a home, child care, even a wedding — dutifully pack our bags, board our flights or fill up our gas tanks, and exercise power where we can.

“We’re in a changing-of-the-guards period,” one friend told me when I asked about her holidays. She has been given more jurisdiction over the menu, which she described as “half staples” and “half experimental vegetables,” which she cooks with her dad. But though she loves to host, she must still decamp to the suburbs. “When you have a baby,” she joked, “everyone will come.”

A Gen Z friend told me his dad “is very serious about Thanksgiving” and “refuses to deviate.” So he found opportunity in lack, pleading to make mac and cheese, a dish absent from their table. Given a green light, he scoured YouTube for inspiration and has made little adjustments over the past decade to arrive at what he believes is perfection. When he suggested bucking convention with a second contribution, though, his dad’s response was like a D.J. mouthing “Sorry, no requests” over a pulsing bass.

As an editor at NYT Cooking who gets to develop recipes, I would love nothing more than to labor over a feast’s worth of new dishes each year and see what sticks. I’ve been itching to introduce a bit more acid to our menu, for example, and break out Alexa Weibel’s roasted mushrooms with smoky pomegranate sauce. But to unseat my father’s beloved wine- and cream-braised mushrooms — which, I gotta say, he always makes far too much of — would have me excommunicated. Even putting that in writing scares me to bits.

My mother hosted her first (albeit small) Thanksgiving when she was 29. She and my father had just moved from Manhattan to Atlanta and were joined at the table by her brother. She labored over the turkey, something she and my grandmother had learned to cook from neighbors when they immigrated from Cuba some 20 years before. She made sweet potato soufflé with Calvados, using a recipe from Gourmet magazine. And she made stuffing dotted with Italian sausage and green bell peppers, of which Dad was not a fan. So went stuffing from the rotation — until, at a far less established 29, I saw my opening. A different stuffing, with challah I make from scratch, has been my contribution to the meal going on five years.

Last year, I developed this recipe for vegan salted maple ginger pie and hoped to squeeze it onto the menu. Alas, dessert is the domain of Uncle Peter, a former pastry chef, who, for nine of us last year, made two whole cakes, including a divine black velvet with Lambeth piping. I should have known better.

Tradition is a comforting anchor when uncertainty swells. But it can be just as soothing to up-anchor and drift. Doing so can serve our appetite for newness (and control). It can also make for a more inclusive meal.

Enter: the vegetarian centerpiece. A mushroom Wellington competes with no aunt’s turkey or ham, offends no one and pleases far more guests than one can imagine. A maple-lacquered pumpkin, stuffed with jeweled rice and lentils and showered with crispy shallots and sage, makes any meatless guest feel like a priority, not an afterthought. The pumpkin is the ideal vessel for such a mission, a symbol of abundance and a critical link in the establishment of Thanksgiving. It’s not just for pie, folks.

At worst, a vegetable preparation envisioned as a main dish will be treated as a side. At best, it is a conversation starter that becomes a hit in its own right. And for the cook who made it, perhaps it grants a sliver of holiday autonomy when so many other markers of adulthood feel out of reach.

THE LATEST NEWS

• The stock market had its worst week in more than a year, with the S&P 500 ending more than 10 percent below its recent high. Tech stocks fared poorly despite Anthropic’s blockbuster I.P.O. as investors showed wariness about the A.I. boom.
• President Trump threatened to ban American tech companies from building data centers outside the U.S., suggesting he could impose a “tremendous tax” or other penalties on violators.
• The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, according to people briefed on the matter.
• Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia spy scandal, has extensive ties to China’s defense industry, The Times found.
• Times Exclusive: ICE went too far last year in loosening its training standards to hire more officers, an internal government watchdog found.
• Federal watchdog lawyers opened an investigation last year into possible fraud surrounding Trump’s memecoin. Then they backed off, convinced the government would kill the inquiry.
• Since losing his Senate bid, Texas’ Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, has dropped a number of high-profile lawsuits against his political opponents.
Around the World
• British and European leaders agreed to remove some of the barriers introduced by Brexit, a decade after the U.K. voted to leave the bloc. Here’s what to know.
• Mexico captured a drug kingpin who was one of the F.B.I.’s 10 most-wanted fugitives, the Mexican government said.
• Polish officials said three Russian objects, including at least one missile, had crashed into the country’s territory. Poland’s prime minister called it an “intentional provocation.”
• An Anthropic mathematician claimed to have proven the Riemann hypothesis, the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, with help from A.I.
• A Missouri state court approved a $7.25 billion nationwide settlement that will end tens of thousands of lawsuits claiming that Bayer’s weedkiller, Roundup, caused cancer.
• ICE agents detained a Chinese-born Princeton neuroscientist while she was traveling from an academic conference.
• The number of new Ph.D. students studying the sciences at major U.S. research institutions has fallen substantially, according to a new federal survey.
ASK THE MORNING
Will the new Democratic majority in Congress be able to limit the war with Iran? | Mark Vezzola | San Diego, California

The Democrats will have a few levers to restrict Trump’s ability to continue the Iran war. They can pass legislation requiring that it end, restrict funding for combat operations or place new restrictions on the Department of Defense. But Trump could veto any of those moves, and Democrats won’t have enough votes to override the president. Even if they refused to approve new defense funding (which could risk a government shutdown), the Pentagon has many ways to shift money around. Democrats’ best chance may come through negotiations where they win concessions on the war in exchange for funding other administration priorities. — Robert Jimison, who covers Congress
THE WEEK IN CULTURE

• Grand Theft Auto VI, which took more than a decade to create, contains a remarkably complex digital world. To illustrate that point, Times reporters examined the myriad options available to players in a single convenience store.
• In the video above, Zachary Small explains how the G.T.A. series evolved to reach this point. Click the video to play.
• The new game is set in Vice City, a fictionalized version of Miami. It is, at its core, about America. Yet the game originated in Scotland.

• Jonathan Yardley, a Pulitzer Prize-winning book critic, died at 87. He reviewed more than 3,000 books, sometimes turning a sharp eye on canonized writers like Steinbeck and Salinger. Read his Times obituary.
• Jan van Eyck, the 15th-century Flemish artist renowned for intimate portraits, helped define a genre. See his genius in three surviving works.
• “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” follows the early years of Haymitch Abernathy, originally played by Woody Harrelson. This new prequel is both bloated and limited, our critic writes.
RECIPE OF THE WEEK
Cranberry Orange Muffins

Most muffins are just cupcakes without frosting, but Yossy Arefi’s cranberry orange muffins are more like tea cakes at heart. These adorable golden-domed treats, made with buttermilk for tang, are topped with a fragrant, orange-zest-flecked glaze. Make them this weekend with any extra cranberries you have on hand. They work equally well with fresh or frozen berries, and they freeze well, too. — Melissa Clark

ADVICE FROM WIRECUTTER
Our most essential travel tips

Heading out of town for the holiday? The right gear and some expert-vetted hacks can make your journey less arduous. For instance, try the 3-to-1 packing method — three tops for every bottom — to avoid overpacking. (By the way, there’s no clear winner in the debate between rolling or folding your clothes.) Bluetooth trackers are great, but don’t overlook the classic luggage tag — it’s the first line of defense against a lost suitcase, and it can help you spot your bag on the carousel. A simple adapter can connect your wireless headphones to the plane’s audio system. And if you’re looking for a great gift for the traveler in your life, our favorites help make flights a bit more comfortable. — Maria Adelmann
GAME OF THE WEEK

Minnesota Vikings vs. San Francisco 49ers: This is one of the most intriguing games of the N.F.L. season. First, there’s the matchup itself: The 49ers have the league’s best offense. The Vikings have the toughest defense, allowing fewer points than any other team. According to The Athletic’s projections, these two teams are the most likely N.F.C. champs. (Here’s a deeper breakdown, plus experts’ predictions.)

And then there’s the venue: Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, which sits at around 7,300 feet above sea level — far higher than even Denver’s vaunted mile-high stadium. The Athletic’s Alec Lewis wrote about the Vikings’ preparations for playing in such extreme altitude, which involved working out in a high-tech environmental chamber. The Niners, for their part, spent the week training in Colorado Springs. Sunday at 8:20 p.m. Eastern on NBC. — Tom Wright-Piersanti
